What 100 Economies Have Taught Us About Climate and Development
text_paragraph_1: The current El Niño is a reminder of how quickly climate shocks can become development challenges. Drought can wither crops and drain the reservoirs that power homes and factories. Heavy rainfall can wash away schools, roads, and other infrastructure. The effects vary from place to place, but the lesson is widely shared: countries need to build resilience through smart development that protects livelihoods, creates jobs, and drives growth.
text_paragraph_2: That is the thinking behind the World Bank Group’s Country Climate and Development Reports (CCDRs). Driven by national development priorities, the series now covers 100 economies, with São Tomé and Príncipe the latest addition . Each CCDR supports countries with a practical roadmap for resilient, low-carbon growth that advances their wider development priorities, from jobs and energy security to better health. They are complemented by annual summary reports that highlight the key global insights, with four reports published so far on infrastructure and the macroeconomy , the interplay with nature and role of forestry, the vulnerability and agency of people , and the implications for jobs .
text_paragraph_3: Reaching 100 economies is a milestone and a good moment to ask what we have learned. I see four lessons and two priorities for the road ahead.

text_paragraph_1: MOCUBA, Mozambique — Mozambique ranks among the 10 countries with the highest deforestation rates in the world. Each year, it loses about 267,000 hectares (660,000 acres) of forest, with the heaviest rates concentrated in the provinces of Nampula, Zambézia, and Manica. To counter this, a decade ago the country set an ambitious goal to reforest 1 million hectares (2.5 million acres) by 2030, alongside a 2025 target to restore 52,000 hectares (128,500 acres) per year through 2029 on a budget of 105 billion meticais ($1.65 billion).
text_paragraph_2: To date, however, only 58,000 hectares (143,300 acres) have been reforested — a total that includes tree plantations established before the million-hectare goal was set, according to data compiled by Sá Nogueira Lisboa, a forestry professor and researcher at Eduardo Mondlane University (UEM) in Maputo.
text_paragraph_3: Zambézia province in central Mozambique holds one of the country’s main forest areas, key to conserving biodiversity, regulating water resources, protecting soil, storing carbon, and supporting local communities. text_paragraph_1: National Bureau of Statistics and Office of the Chief Government Statistician, The Labour Market: Key Findings from the Integrated Labour Force Survey 2025, June 2026. The survey covered Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar and was conducted between January and December 2025. The labour force participation and employment rates improved in 2025, but 95.7 percent of workers remain in informal employment, agriculture still employs more than half the workforce and only 13.2 percent of workers hold paid jobs.
text_paragraph_2: Tanzania’s labour market absorbed more people into economic activity in 2025, with both labour force participation and the employment to population ratio rising from a year earlier, but the structure of work remains overwhelmingly informal, leaving the economy with a large number of people who are technically employed without necessarily having stable wages, formal contracts, social protection or the productivity gains associated with more structured employment.
text_paragraph_3: The 2025 Integrated Labour Force Survey , conducted jointly across Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar and published by the National Bureau of Statistics and the Office of the Chief Government Statistician, shows the labour force participation rate increasing from 73.2 percent in 2024 to 75.9 percent in 2025, while the employment to population ratio rose from 68.7 percent to 71.4 percent. The survey, which covered 14,232 households and 60,889 individuals with a response rate of 99.63 percent, therefore points to stronger labour absorption during the year and a larger proportion of working age Tanzanians participating in economic activity.

text_paragraph_1: Tanzania’s informal sector generated TZS 88.1 trillion in value added in 2025, equivalent to 36.3 percent of GDP, while supporting nearly 24 million workers and 64 percent of households. The country's first nationwide informal sector survey estimates that informal activity generates more than one-third of GDP, showing that informality is one of the country’s largest economic systems rather than a marginal part of the economy.
text_paragraph_2: Tanzania’s informal sector generated TZS 88.1 trillion in gross value added in 2025, equivalent to 36.3 percent of national GDP, providing one of the clearest official measurements yet of the scale at which economic activity takes place outside conventional formal business structures and showing that informality is not a peripheral feature of the economy but one of its largest operating systems.
text_paragraph_3: The figure comes from the Tanzania Informal Sector Survey 2025 , the first nationally representative survey of its kind covering both Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar through a collaborative effort between the National Bureau of Statistics and the Office of the Chief Government Statistician. The survey was designed to measure informal sector employment, production, income, business structure, access to finance and the sector’s contribution to GDP, filling a long standing data gap around economic activity that is often poorly captured because enterprises operate with limited records, low levels of organisation and little or no formal registration.

text_paragraph_1: INFLATION is the sustained rise in the prices of goods and services across an economy over time. It reduces the purchasing power of money and alters business investment, and its relationship with economic growth depends heavily on how fast prices rise.
text_paragraph_2: It is driven mainly by three factors: demand-pull, cost-push and growth in the money supply. Demand-pull pressure arises when consumer or government demand for goods and services outpaces the economy’s ability to produce them. This reflects the familiar idea that too much money is chasing too few goods, a situation fuelled by rising incomes, cheaper borrowing and government stimulus.
text_paragraph_3: Rising prices are inevitable wherever goods are scarce, and in recent years they have been climbing at their fastest pace in many countries. When inflation is high, the money a buyer saves today will be worth less in the future, and people feel the damage most directly when prices rise too sharply.

The title of the SIEPR Policy Forum said it all: “ Unlocking Africa’s Economic Potential .”
text_paragraph_3: Statistics shared during the daylong event signal there’s a lot to be excited about. For example, Africa will have the world’s youngest and largest workforce by 2035; by century’s end, 40% of the global population will call the continent home. By 2040, Africa will count 12 cities with populations of 10 million or more, up from two today. An investment boom underway before the Iran war has strengthened as firms look beyond the Middle East to meet demand for oil and fertilizers. A historic free trade agreement promises to open up trade across the region. And artificial intelligence could unleash a wave of tech-savvy entrepreneurs and, in the process, rewrite the emerging country playbook for growth.

text_paragraph_1: Life unfolds in motion in Cumpanghor, a village in Guinea-Bissau 's eastern Gabu region. Women tend vegetable gardens, chickens cluck inside a newly built poultry house, and young girls and boys learn to sew clothes in a once-abandoned community centre. These snapshots of village life are part of a single, far-reaching experiment in building grassroots resilience and food security.
text_paragraph_2: What started as a few sewing machines to build skills in 2024 has since evolved into a broader community effort. After the sewing came poultry farming in Cumpanghor, followed by training in horticulture and irrigation – and the installation of a solar-powered pump and overhead storage tank. As gardens began to flourish and eggs reached the market, school meals arrived, reconnecting children's nutrition with food produced by the community.
text_paragraph_3: The transformation is part of One SDG Tabanca Initiative at a Time, a project launched by the World Food Programme (WFP) in collaboration with regional authorities and a local women’s farming cooperative, CAMUCA. In Guinea-Bissau’s Creole language, tabanca means village. And Cumpanghor is ground zero for the pilot, which aims to support one community at a time through interconnected activities.

Constitutional Court to host meeting of Bureau of Association of Francophone Constitutional Courts next week
text_paragraph_1: The Constitutional Court of Romania (CCR) will host a meeting of the Bureau of the Association of Francophone Constitutional Courts (ACCF), as well as a working session themed 'The Information Society and Constitutional Democracy' next Friday. According to a press release issued by the Constitutional Court of Romania to AGERPRES on Friday, the Court is currently holding the presidency of the ACCF for a three-year term (2025-2028). It is the third constitutional jurisdiction in Europe to hold this position, following those of France (1997-2000) and Switzerland (2015-2019). In 2027, under the CCR's presidency, the ACCF will mark the 30th anniversary of its founding. 'The two events will take place at the Palace of the Parliament, in the Human Rights Hall, and will bring together high-level representatives from the constitutional jurisdictions of 10 countries, alongside the Constitutional Court of Romania, providing a framework for international institutional dialogue and cooperation,' the statement notes. President Nicusor Dan has been invited to attend the working session, the source adds. The release further indicates that the Bureau's proceedings will involve representatives from the constitutional jurisdictions of Romania, Benin, Gabon, Albania, Belgium, Cambodia, Mauritania, France, and Senegal, as well as a representative from the ACCF General Secretariat. The working meeting will also involve the participation of representatives from the Constitutional Court of Austria and the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Moldova, alongside the justices of the Constitutional Court of Romania. The theme of the working meeting, 'The Information Society and Constitutional Democracy,' addresses the increasingly significant role of information and technology across all spheres of human life, as well as the profound transformations within the information society that also impact the mechanisms of constitutional democracy, the Constitutional Court of Romania reports. The Association of Francophone Constitutional Courts (ACCF), founded in 1997, has consistently promoted institutional dialogue regarding the development of constitutional justice, the strengthening of democracy, the rule of law, and human rights. It has achieved this by fostering relations among members within the Francophone sphere, both through its own events and by collaborating with various international forums and organizations. The Association of Francophone Constitutional Courts brings together 50 constitutional courts and equivalent institutions (comprising 47 members and 3 observers) from Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Asia. Established in 1997 at the initiative of the French Constitutional Council under the name 'Association of Constitutional Courts Using the French Language' (ACCPUF), the organization became the Association of Francophone Constitutional Courts (ACCF) in 2019. In May 2025, the Constitutional Court of Romania was selected by the member jurisdictions, convened in a general assembly, to hold the 10th presidency of the ACCF. The Constitutional Court of Romania became a full member of the ACCPUF in 1998 and it has been a member of the ACCF Bureau since 2022 and served as vice-president from 2022 to 2025. title: Sao Tome: The sweet comeback of vanilla

text_paragraph_2: To boost his income, the farmer recently began growing vanilla. On Sao Tome, which is best known for its cocoa, the spice is currently making a comeback. Cette brève présence sera également mise à profit pour organiser des activités de formation, a indiqué le porte-parole. Cette opération s’inscrit dans le cadre d’un exercice militaire conjoint prévu en novembre, auquel participeront les forces armées de la Côte d’Ivoire, du Gabon et de la France. Lors de la visite de Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno à Paris, en octobre, les deux pays avaient signé une déclaration d’intention destinée à définir les nouvelles bases de leur coopération en matière de défense. text_paragraph_2: What started as a few sewing machines to build skills in 2024 has since evolved into a broader community effort. Ethiopia: FAJ survey reveals poverty, fear and censorship have pushed African journalism into crisis
text_paragraph_1: The Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) launched its Survey on  the working conditions of journalists in Africa on 25 October in the Ethiopia Capital, Addis Ababa.  Drawing responses from 1,586 journalists in 45 countries across the continent’s five regions, the survey report revealed how poverty wages, insecure employment and threats combine to weaken journalism and restricts the public’s access to information and their right to know.
text_paragraph_2: The report entitled "Journalism Under Siege: Abysmal Working Conditions and the Decline of Media Freedom in Africa" is the first journalist-led continental report to bring together evidence on journalists’ working conditions, labour rights, safety and media freedom. It is based on a survey conducted by FAJ with support from UNESCO’s Multi-Donor Programme on Freedom of Expression and Safety of Journalists. “The findings of this report expose a profession in deep crisis. Journalists are expected to inform the public while struggling to survive. These are not separate problems: poverty, insecure work and threats are pushing journalism towards silence. When journalists cannot earn a living, work safely or report freely, media freedom exists only on paper, and the public is denied the information it needs. According to the report,  61% of respondents said their income from journalism does not meet their basic living needs, while only 4% said their salaries adequately cover essential costs. Fifty-eight percent reported delayed salaries, 62% worked without written contracts and 71% lacked social protection. Freelance journalists made up 29% of respondents, while contributors and stringers accounted for a further 18%. More than half of those surveyed, 53%, were aged between 18 and 34. The report also documents the threats journalists face. Sixty-five percent had experienced threats or intimidation linked to their work in the past three years. Only 17% always feel safe reporting, while 55% rarely or never felt safe. It also notes that at least 18 journalists and media workers were killed in Africa in 2025 in connection with their work, according to the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ). “The pressure on journalism is not confined to physical attacks. It also comes through legal intimidation, censorship and barriers to information. When journalists are punished, threatened or pushed out of work for reporting in the public interest, the whole of society loses. Governments and media organisations must protect journalists’ safety, independence and right to work” said FAJ President, Omar Faruk Osman. The findings show how these pressures affect editorial decisions. Eighty-four percent of respondents said they practised self-censorship frequently or occasionally, and 69% said threats had led them to avoid certain stories. Respondents identified political interference (29%), violence against journalists (22%) and restrictive laws (18%) as the most critical threats to media freedom. Among the violations they had experienced, respondents reported political interference (68%), barriers to accessing information (61%), censorship (57%), legal intimidation (49%) and internet shutdowns affecting reporting (23%). Only 6% described media freedom in their country as “very free”, while 65% said it was restricted or highly restricted. Digital threats also add to these pressures. Thirty-six percent of respondents had experienced online harassment linked to their journalism work, 26% digital surveillance, 24% experienced sexual abuse online  and 21%  experienced hacking attempts. Yet 63% had received no digital safety training. More than three-quarters of respondents, 76%, said women journalists face additional risks, including sexual harassment, online gender-based violence, unequal pay, workplace discrimination, exclusion from leadership and intimidation connected to political or investigative reporting. The findings also revealed a serious strain on journalists’ wellbeing and the future of the profession. Financial insecurity was the most commonly reported source of stress (38%), followed by fear of attacks (24%). Seventy-two percent said their workplaces provided no mental health or counselling support, 44% reported frequent burnout and 47% had considered leaving journalism. The report warns that losing journalists, including younger professionals, could further weaken investigative reporting, public accountability and access to reliable information. FAJ emphasised that the findings call for urgent and concrete actions from governments, media employers and relevant institutions. The report calls for fair wages, written contracts, social protection and safe workplaces; prompt investigations into attacks and an end to impunity; and reform of laws used to intimidate or criminalise journalists. It also urges stronger protection mechanisms, respect for editorial independence, collective bargaining and social dialogue, digital safety support and specific measures to protect women journalists.

What the 2023/2024 El Niño season reveals about climate resilience
text_paragraph_1: The 2023/2024 El Niño brought one of the worst droughts Southern Africa has seen in decades. When drought is that severe, the question is no longer simply whether a crop is “drought tolerant.” It is how much production can be protected, for which farmers, under what conditions, and whether that is enough to soften the blow to food security. Two recent studies led by CIMMYT scientists , both drawing lessons from the devastating El Niño in the 2023/2024 agricultural year in Southern Africa, approach this question from different directions but arrive at similar conclusions. One examines how different crops responded to the 2023/2024 El Niño induced drought across agroecological zones in Zambia. The other looks more closely at farms and households in Zimbabwe, examining whether stress-tolerant maize delivered benefits evenly across smallholder farmers.
text_paragraph_2: Read together, they suggest that climate resilience is more complicated than it often sounds. No single crop, variety, or technology can remove the risk posed by an extreme El Niño. But crop diversification, improved varieties and effective agronomic management can reduce some of that risk, sometimes by margins that are highly consequential for farming households.
text_paragraph_3: The Zambia study, “ Crop-specific impacts of the 2023/2024 drought on Zambia’s agricultural production ” published in the Journal Climate Services, examines district-level production alongside 30 years of rainfall data. The results show how unevenly drought affects crops. A season with substantially below-average rainfall (one standard deviation below the 30-year mean) was associated with estimated yield losses of about 30% for maize, compared with 9% for sorghum and 12% for millet. Rice and sweet potato also suffered relatively large losses, while sunflower, cowpea, common bean and groundnut showed greater resilience than soybean and Bambara nut.

text_paragraph_1: Life unfolds in motion in Cumpanghor, a village in Guinea-Bissau 's eastern Gabu region. Women tend vegetable gardens, chickens cluck inside a newly built poultry house, and young girls and boys learn to sew clothes in a once-abandoned community centre. These snapshots of village life are part of a single, far-reaching experiment in building grassroots resilience and food security.
text_paragraph_2: What started as a few sewing machines to build skills in 2024 has since evolved into a broader community effort. After the sewing came poultry farming in Cumpanghor, followed by training in horticulture and irrigation – and the installation of a solar-powered pump and overhead storage tank. As gardens began to flourish and eggs reached the market, school meals arrived, reconnecting children's nutrition with food produced by the community.
text_paragraph_3: The transformation is part of One SDG Tabanca Initiative at a Time, a project launched by the World Food Programme (WFP) in collaboration with regional authorities and a local women’s farming cooperative, CAMUCA. In Guinea-Bissau’s Creole language, tabanca means village. And Cumpanghor is ground zero for the pilot, which aims to support one community at a time through interconnected activities.

text_paragraph_1: IdeasLAB Think Piece | By Sigame Boubacar Maiga , École Normale Supérieure de Bamako, Mali
text_paragraph_2: Linguistic justice has become a major issue in shaping the future of education in Africa. Despite the achievement of independence, colonial languages continue to dominate educational systems, scientific research and mechanisms of social mobility. This situation raises fundamental questions about equity, educational sovereignty and the place of African languages in the production and transmission of knowledge. In a context shaped by globalization and the influence of multilateral organizations, it is essential to examine the relationship between global education governance, international cooperation, and linguistic diversity.
text_paragraph_3: How, then, can the demands of international integration be reconciled with the recognition and promotion of African languages and cultures? This think piece examines the challenges of linguistic justice across the continent, focusing on educational policies, international cooperation, and the case of Mali. It seeks to identify pathways towards a more inclusive and equitable model of educational governance that respects linguistic pluralism and recognizes Africa’s linguistic diversity as a valuable resource for educational development and the democratization of knowledge.

text_paragraph_1: ‎The Niger State House of Assembly has commended troops of the Nigerian Army for repelling a major attack by bandits on communities in Rafi Local Government Area of the state, which left one soldier dead and three others injured. ‎ ‎The House also called for the establishment of additional military bases in vulnerable communities to strengthen security, prevent bandits from regrouping, and improve rapid response to distress calls. ‎ ‎The commendation followed a motion moved by the member representing Rafi Constituency, Zubairu Zanna, during plenary on Tuesday. ‎ ‎The lawmaker praised the troops for their courage, professionalism and gallantry in confronting the armed men, saying their intervention prevented what could have resulted in a massacre of innocent residents.
text_paragraph_2: ‎ About two weeks ago, more than 100 suspected bandits reportedly invaded communities along the Zungeru-Tegina Road but were met with stiff resistance from the Army, which successfully repelled the attack. ‎ ‎Although one soldier reportedly died from gunshot injuries while three others sustained injuries, several bandits were neutralised during the encounter, and motorcycles were recovered. ‎ ‎Zanna urged the Nigerian Army and other security agencies to sustain their operations and strengthen their presence in the affected communities to prevent further attacks. ‎ ‎He stressed the strategic and economic importance of the communities, noting that the establishment of a Forward Operating Base (FOB) would help prevent criminal groups from regrouping and launching fresh attacks. ‎ ‎According to him, the absence of military bases and strategically positioned security formations along identified vulnerable corridors could limit the ability of security personnel to respond swiftly to distress calls. ‎ ‎The lawmaker further observed that difficult terrain, extensive forests and inadequately secured rural routes in parts of the state, particularly Rafi Local Government Area, provided opportunities for criminal groups to infiltrate communities, establish camps and hideouts, and launch attacks on innocent residents. ‎ ‎He therefore called on the Niger State Government to urgently engage the Federal Government on the need to establish additional military bases and strengthen security deployments in vulnerable communities, particularly along routes frequently used by bandits. ‎ ‎The Speaker of the House, Abdulmalik Sarkindaji, who presided over the plenary, called for a minute of silence in honour of the fallen soldier and offered prayers for the speedy recovery of those receiving medical treatment.
